title: The Cooling Break
subject: The 2026 World Cup
voice_note: Written in the voice of Ernest Hemingway (1899–1961), through the writer-hemingway skill. An emulation — the prose and judgments are not the historical Hemingway's own words. The scores, dates, temperatures, and quotations are drawn from verified reporting on the tournament as of July 2, 2026.
body:
In the summer of that year the World Cup came to North America and they played it in the heat. There were sixteen stadiums across the three countries. Three of them, in Dallas and Houston and Atlanta, had roofs and cooled air, and the other thirteen were open to the sun. The grass had been grown for ten months on farms in North Carolina and hauled to the stadiums in refrigerated trucks and laid down over the football fields, and Rabiot said it played hard and rigid, and Vinicius said it dried out fast and the game went slow on it. Spain flew seven thousand eight hundred miles in the group stage and won the group anyway. France flew three hundred and thirty-four. It was the biggest country a World Cup had ever been played in, and the teams crossed it in airplanes between the matches, and at the end of June the great heat came up over the east and lay on Philadelphia and Boston and Kansas City and New York and did not lift at night. The weather service said the nights would not offer any relief. That was the country the football was played in.

Twice in every match now the referee stops the play so the men can drink. It is in the rules this year for the first time. The play stops for three minutes in the twenty-second minute and again in the sixty-seventh, in all the hundred and four matches, whatever the weather. The coaches do not care for it. Tuchel, who has England, said he liked football more when it was two halves. Deschamps, who has France, said it is almost four quarters now. At the stops the men drink and pull ice vests on over their shirts and put chilled collars on their necks, and then the whistle goes and they play again. The matches go off at noon and in the middle of the afternoon because afternoon in America is evening in Europe, and the television is in Europe. The players' union said the afternoons in Kansas City and Miami and Monterrey were extremely high risk. The kickoff times stayed where they were.

In Miami the first match went off at six in the evening on the fifteenth of June, Saudi Arabia against Uruguay. It was ninety degrees at the kick and in the stands you sweated standing still. The fire rescue took ten calls for heat that evening and carried two people to the hospital. Over the first four matches at Hard Rock Stadium the county logged thirty-seven heat calls and five transports. The night Brazil played Scotland it was eighty-one degrees, and there were no calls. When Colombia played Portugal there at the end of June, nothing to nothing, it was close to ninety at half past seven in the evening, and the Colombians sat through the water breaks in ice vests and the Portuguese wore the chilled collars.

In Foxborough on the thirteenth of June a young Scottish winger named Ben Gannon-Doak came off after seventy-five minutes against Haiti with both calves cramped. "Both my calf muscles decided to leave the stadium before me," he said. Scotland won that night, 1–0, and went out in the group anyway. Uruguay went out too, two points, the highest-ranked team to go home before the knockouts, and it was their own goalkeeper's mistake against Spain that finished them. No player has gone down on the field from the heat. When the doctors are asked about that they reach back to Houston in 2017 for the last one who did. There are two and a half weeks still to run, and the hottest days have only now arrived.

Twice the lightning has stopped it. In Philadelphia on the twenty-second of June they sent France and Iraq to the dressing rooms at the half, at ten minutes to six, and the crowd stood in the concourses for two hours and eleven minutes while the storm worked through. The rule says lightning inside eight miles stops the match for thirty minutes, and every new strike starts the thirty minutes over, and there is no rule for when it ends. France came back out and won 3–0. In Mexico City the storm came down two hours before Mexico played Ecuador at the Azteca, thunder and hard rain, and the kickoff went back an hour, and eighty thousand people danced in ponchos while they waited. Mexico won 2–0, Quiñones and Jiménez, their first knockout win in forty years, and no one has ever beaten Mexico at the Azteca in a World Cup. England comes there Sunday. The Azteca sits at seven thousand two hundred feet and there is less air in it, and Tuchel said you cannot physically adapt to it, so England will fly in two days before the match to keep clear of the days when the altitude does its worst work. Kane scored twice in the last fifteen minutes in Atlanta to get them there.

The twenty-ninth of June was the day of the penalties. In Foxborough, Paraguay and Germany stood 1–1 after the extra time. Enciso had scored before the half and Havertz had headed the equalizer, and in the extra time Tah put the ball in the net and the video took the goal away. Then the kicks. The Paraguayan goalkeeper is named Orlando Gill. He saved from Havertz and he saved from Woltemade, and Tah, whose goal had been taken away, put the last kick over the bar. Germany had never lost a penalty shootout at a World Cup. They have lost one now. The same evening in Monterrey, in the hottest stadium of the sixteen, Morocco and the Netherlands stood 1–1, Gakpo in the seventy-second minute and Diop in the first minute of added time, and in the shootout Bounou saved the fourth Dutch kick and Saibari struck the winner. Morocco plays Canada in Houston on the Fourth of July, indoors, in the cooled air. Forty-two men from one Moroccan supporters' club asked the United States for visas to follow their team. Two got them.

All three hosts are still in it. Canada had never won a knockout match and won one in Los Angeles, 1–0 over South Africa, Eustáquio in stoppage time. The United States beat Bosnia 2–0 at Santa Clara with ten men. Balogun scored the first and the video sent him off in the sixty-fourth minute, and Tillman put a free kick in to finish it. There is no appeal from the video. Balogun will watch the Belgium match in Seattle on the sixth from the stands.

There are old men in it too. Messi is thirty-nine. He has six goals here, he has scored in seven straight World Cup matches, which no man had done, and no man has scored more at World Cups than he has now. The sixth was a free kick against Jordan after they sent him on from the bench. Mbappé has six as well, two of them against Sweden at the Meadowlands. Ronaldo is forty-one and scored at his sixth World Cup, the first man to do that, and tonight in Toronto his Portugal plays Croatia and Modrić, who is forty. It was not settled when this was written. And there is Cape Verde. Cape Verde is a group of islands off West Africa with five hundred and twenty-five thousand people on them, at their first World Cup, and they went through a group that held Spain and Uruguay without losing a match. Their goalkeeper is called Vozinha and he is forty years old, and he made seven saves the night they held Spain to nothing in Atlanta. Tomorrow they play Argentina in Miami. In Miami it will be hot.

The president of FIFA came to New York the week before the knockouts and said that this was bigger than anything the world had ever seen, not just any football event but any event in any way, the most successful event in history. Before it began he had said that the people who worried should chill and relax. The cheapest seat that can be bought for the final costs about ten thousand three hundred dollars. The final is on the nineteenth of July at the Meadowlands, and the Meadowlands has no roof.

On the Fourth of July, France plays Paraguay in Philadelphia at five in the afternoon. The forecast is one hundred degrees. The weather men are calling it the hottest and most dangerous game of the whole World Cup, hotter than anything in Miami. The referee will stop it in the twenty-second minute and again in the sixty-seventh so the men can drink, and the rest of it they will play in the sun.
